title: When It Comes to Rewards, the Longer the Delay, the Less the Perceived Value
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay applies the behavioral-science concept of delayed-reward discounting to workplace motivation, explaining that people mentally shrink the value of a reward the longer they must wait for it -- undermining effort over time in organizations built around long-delayed payoffs. It offers three concrete countermeasures for leaders: breaking large rewards into smaller milestone-based pieces, leaning more on intrinsic motivators (skill investment, purpose, autonomy) rather than pure extrinsic reward, and periodically reminding the team of the reward's real value through stories of past beneficiaries. The piece frames this as a practical toolkit for sustaining motivation across long project timelines.
points: Delayed-reward discounting means people mentally shrink the perceived value of a reward the longer they must wait for it.
Most workplaces are 'delayed gratification factories,' asking for effort now in exchange for rewards far in the future.
Breaking rewards into smaller milestone payouts throughout the year reduces the impact of discounting.
Leaning on intrinsic motivators -- skill-building, purpose, autonomy -- helps offset the decay in perceived reward value.
Regularly reminding teams of the reward's real value, using stories of past beneficiaries, disrupts the discounting effect.
quotes: The inability to delay gratification is a common weakness for many people.
Less commonly known is how people slash the value of a delayed reward over time.
Behavioral scientists call this delayed-reward discounting, and it represents a huge challenge for leaders.
Leaders who depend primarily on delayed rewards to motivate team members often find both effort and work quality suffer over time.

More intrinsic motivators such as investing in team member skills, elevating the higher purpose of the work, and giving people more autonomy or control over their assignments can help offset the discounting effect.
Best of all, proven through their example is that the rewards are less important than the opportunity to learn and work alongside amazing people.
